sections.text: WS-POL-I – Citation, Disclosure, and Process Evidence Analysis

The strongest overall conclusion is that WS-POL-I is one of the committee’s clearest transparency sections, but not one of its clearest consensus sections. There is broad agreement that students should not hide meaningful AI assistance and that FCCPS needs some disclosure expectations. There is not broad agreement on how much must be disclosed, when, by whom, and whether process evidence such as chat logs, drafts, checkpoints, or other workflow artifacts should be required as a routine expectation or only in selected contexts. The outline captures that directly: “There is general agreement that transparency around AI use is important. However, there is no consensus on requiring submission of chat logs.”

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: Meeting 3 helps explain why this section became so important. The committee repeatedly returned to the problem that AI can produce polished products that obscure what students actually know and can do. Elizabeth Chua warned that when students use AI as a tutor or to polish their writing, teachers may lose the feedback signal they need to understand where students really are in the learning process. John Black then linked that to assessment design and to the risk that poorly structured assignments can create a kind of competitive coercion to use AI. That conversation naturally leads to WS-POL-I: if product alone is no longer enough, what kinds of citation, disclosure, and process evidence are necessary to make learning visible again? (Meeting 3 transcript)

heading_path: How the committee got here
sections.text: The survey shows that this issue had already crystallized by the time the committee moved into structured tradeoff language. The survey tested principles and postures for student disclosure, use transparency, design before bans, prevent cognitive offloading, visible thinking, and a tradeoff question on disclosure. That means WS-POL-I was never only about citation style. It sat at the junction of academic integrity, fairness, teacher workload, developmental appropriateness, and privacy. (Survey export)

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: The strongest committee agreement is on transparency as a principle. Multiple survey respondents approved or lightly revised statements like:

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: “Student disclosure. FCCPS will set grade-banded expectations for when and how students disclose AI assistance,”

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text:
and “Use transparency. FCCPS will set clear expectations for when students and staff disclose AI assistance in school work.”
Even respondents who objected to wording often did not object to disclosure in principle. Their objections were mainly about granularity, feasibility, or the wrong variables being used.

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: The V3 outline reflects that same center of gravity. It states:

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: students should acknowledge meaningful AI assistance when it contributes to ideas, structure, or content,

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: expectations should be developmentally appropriate and aligned with assignment goals and subject-area norms,

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: disclosure expectations should define what counts as meaningful AI assistance,

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: and communication to students must be clear enough to avoid confusion across classrooms.

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: A second area of convergence is that one-size-fits-all rules are risky. Even among respondents who favored stronger disclosure, several emphasized that disclosure depends on grade band, stakes, subject, and what the student actually used AI for. One of the clearest survey responses in the middle camp supported grade-banded disclosure, strongest for high-stakes work, and explicitly tied that to developmental appropriateness and feasibility. Another emphasized that expectations should be “simple and teachable,” for example a checkbox plus short reflection when AI meaningfully shaped ideas, structure, or analysis. (Survey export)

heading_path: Where agreement appears strongest
sections.text: A third area of broad agreement is that process evidence can be useful, but that the committee is divided on how formalized it should become. The outline’s own phrasing treats this as a tradeoff rather than a settled norm: transparency versus privacy, practicality and burden on teachers, and the risk of over-standardizing diverse classroom practices.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Universal disclosure vs. contextual disclosure
sections.text: This is the clearest split in the accessible record.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Universal disclosure vs. contextual disclosure
sections.text: A more restrictive and transparency-maximizing view argues for broad disclosure of any AI use. One survey respondent asked bluntly, “What is the argument against disclosure?” Another said the same disclosure rules should apply regardless of grade if a student is writing an essay. That camp sees disclosure as the default ethical baseline and tends to distrust attempts to create too many exceptions.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
1. Universal disclosure vs. contextual disclosure
sections.text: A more contextual view supports disclosure, but only when AI use is meaningful or material, or especially in high-stakes work. Several respondents preferred grade-banded disclosure or disclosure only when AI meaningfully shapes content, analysis, or structure. This camp is worried that universal disclosure rules can become noisy, burdensome, and insensitive to educational context. That middle position is probably the committee’s center of gravity, because it matches both the V3 outline and several survey responses. (Survey export)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
2. Grade-banded disclosure vs. common district-wide rules
sections.text: The committee clearly agrees that age and context matter, but there is real disagreement about whether that should produce different disclosure requirements by grade band.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
2. Grade-banded disclosure vs. common district-wide rules
sections.text: The outline leans toward grade-banded disclosure. So do several survey responses, especially those aligned with the design-first middle. They argue that disclosure expectations should be developmentally appropriate and proportionate to stakes.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
2. Grade-banded disclosure vs. common district-wide rules
sections.text: But one more restrictive respondent objected that different grade bands do not necessarily need different disclosure requirements, arguing that if a student is writing an essay, the same disclosure obligation may apply regardless of grade. That is a good example of a recurring committee divide: developmental tailoring versus cross-district clarity. (Survey export)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
3. Process evidence as design support vs. process evidence as surveillance burden
sections.text: This is probably the most important conceptual split inside WS-POL-I.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
3. Process evidence as design support vs. process evidence as surveillance burden
sections.text: One camp sees process evidence—drafts, checkpoints, annotations, oral defense, reflections, or even chat logs—as part of a design-first approach to preserving validity. In the survey, the strongest middle respondents favored “design before bans,” saying FCCPS should protect assessment validity primarily through assessment design and process evidence, and apply restrictions only where validity cannot otherwise be preserved. For this camp, process evidence is not mainly about catching students after the fact. It is about structuring learning so authentic thinking remains visible.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
3. Process evidence as design support vs. process evidence as surveillance burden
sections.text: The opposing camp is highly skeptical of this move. One survey response said process evidence is “easily fakable by AI” and rejected the “design versus restriction” framing as false because design constraints are themselves restrictions. That same respondent saw disclosure and process expectations as too dependent on undefined terms like “high-stakes” and too vulnerable to manipulation. This is a very important critique for your drafting because it means some committee members will not be reassured by arguments that process evidence is a softer alternative to restrictions. They may see it as both weaker and more ambiguous. (Survey export)

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Chat logs specifically: no consensus
sections.text: This is the one point the outline makes completely explicit: no consensus on requiring submission of chat logs.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Chat logs specifically: no consensus
sections.text: The survey helps explain why. Some respondents wanted stronger transparency and appeared open to substantial evidence requirements. But others viewed anything resembling routine workflow submission as intrusive, impractical, or educationally unhelpful. Even many middle-position responses that favored design/process evidence did not endorse blanket log requirements. Their emphasis was usually on proportionate, assignment-specific evidence rather than universal logging.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Chat logs specifically: no consensus
sections.text: So the committee’s actual divide is not simply “for or against chat logs.” It is more like:

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Chat logs specifically: no consensus
sections.text: no logs and no routine process documentation,

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Chat logs specifically: no consensus
sections.text: selective process evidence in specific contexts,

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Chat logs specifically: no consensus
sections.text: or stronger, more universal transparency expectations.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
4. Chat logs specifically: no consensus
sections.text: The accessible record suggests the middle option has the most support, while routine chat-log submission does not.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
5. Citation vs. disclosure
sections.text: This issue is more visible in other committee materials than in the survey alone, but the survey still reinforces it. Several principles and comments distinguish between acknowledging AI assistance and giving educators enough information to evaluate student work fairly. That maps closely onto the conceptual difference the committee has already been drawing elsewhere between citation as acknowledgment and disclosure as evaluative transparency.

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
5. Citation vs. disclosure
sections.text: The practical implication for WS-POL-I is that “citation” and “disclosure” should probably not be collapsed into a single undifferentiated requirement. The committee seems to want students to do both kinds of work:

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
5. Citation vs. disclosure
sections.text: acknowledge meaningful assistance,

heading_path: Main fault lines and the range of opinions
5. Citation vs. disclosure
sections.text: and make enough of their use visible for teachers to assess learning fairly.

heading_path: What the survey says most clearly
sections.text: The survey gives a fairly clean picture of three clusters.

heading_path: What the survey says most clearly
sections.text: A restriction-first / maximal-transparency cluster wants strong disclosure, is skeptical of process evidence as a substitute for restriction, rejects detectors, and wants fewer vague or context-sensitive standards.

heading_path: What the survey says most clearly
sections.text: A design-first / grade-banded transparency cluster supports disclosure and process evidence as part of learning design, wants the strongest expectations in high-stakes contexts, and prefers flexibility calibrated by grade band, subject, and task.

heading_path: What the survey says most clearly
sections.text: A more permissive / workload-sensitive cluster still supports transparency in principle, but worries more about overburdening teachers and students, and is more open to contextual flexibility, lighter disclosure, and optional use cases so long as learning goals are preserved.

heading_path: What the survey says most clearly
sections.text: The strongest evidence for the middle cluster comes from respondents who chose:

heading_path: What the survey says most clearly
sections.text: Option C on policy posture: design/process evidence first,

heading_path: What the survey says most clearly
sections.text: Option C on detectors: advisory only,

heading_path: What the survey says most clearly
sections.text:
and grade-banded or high-stakes-focused disclosure models.
That cluster appears to be the most aligned with the wording that ultimately made it into V3. (Survey export)

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: For WS-POL-I, the strongest committee-grounded common ground is:

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: FCCPS should require some form of transparency around meaningful AI use.

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: Students should not present meaningful AI assistance as invisible.

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: Disclosure expectations should be clear enough to teach and apply.

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: Expectations should probably vary by grade band, task type, and stakes, even if members disagree on how much.

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: Process evidence may play a role, but the committee does not support a simple blanket rule requiring chat logs for everything.

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: Any disclosure/process-evidence model must balance fairness, privacy, feasibility, and instructional value.

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: Where you will need to choose your own position is on three questions:

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: whether disclosure should be triggered by any AI use or only meaningful AI assistance,

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: how far to go on grade-banded and high-stakes differentiation,

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: and whether process evidence should be treated mainly as a design tool or as an integrity backstop.

heading_path: What this means for your drafting
sections.text: The next clean step is a WS-POL-I chair preface, followed by your member contribution for that section.
